findings.title: Backup code consumption is not atomic, allowing a code to be reused
findings.body: The backup-code validation reads the encrypted backupCodes blob, decrypts it, finds a matching code, and then writes back the updated list with that entry nulled out (lines 131-156). This read-decrypt-modify-write sequence is not performed inside a transaction or with any locking/compare-and-swap. If two requests present the same backup code concurrently (e.g. an attacker retrying, or a double form submission), both can read the code as still valid before either write completes, so the same backup code can authenticate twice. This defeats the stated guarantee ("each backup code can be used exactly once") and is a security-relevant data integrity bug.

findings.title: Backup codes stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of one-way hashing
findings.body: Backup codes are generated in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts and stored via symmetricEncrypt (reversible) using CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, the same key used for the TOTP secret. Unlike passwords, which are hashed one-way, backup codes act as long-lived authentication secrets (similar to passwords) and should be hashed (e.g. bcrypt/argon2) rather than symmetrically encrypted. If the encryption key and database are both compromised, all users' backup codes can be recovered in plaintext, allowing full account takeover bypassing 2FA. This is a weaker security posture than expected for a credential of this type.

findings.title: Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes screen leaves UI state out of sync with the server
findings.body: After the TOTP is verified, the server has already enabled 2FA (handleEnable sets step to SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes without calling onEnable()). The onEnable() callback that informs the parent component that 2FA is enabled is now only invoked when the user explicitly clicks the 'Close' button (data-testid="backup-codes-close", lines 261-272). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking the overlay, navigating away and back, etc. via the Dialog's onOpenChange), onEnable() is never called and resetState() never runs, so the parent's UI (e.g. the two-factor switch) can remain stale/unchecked even though 2FA is actually enabled server-side. Previously, onEnable() fired immediately on successful verification, so this inconsistency window did not exist.

findings.title: No e2e coverage for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: The PR's stated purpose is to enable backup codes for 2FA login and disable flows, but the added test only exercises the download/copy/close UI actions on the backup-codes screen during setup (lines 110-125). There is no test that actually submits a backup code via the 'Lost access' flow on the login page or the disable-2FA modal, which is the core new functionality described in the PR (and explicitly called out as missing via the 'TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup' comment at line 12). This leaves the primary new feature (backup code authentication) completely untested.

findings.title: backupCodes state is implicitly typed as never[], losing type safety
findings.body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` has no generic type argument, so TypeScript infers backupCodes as `never[]`. Although `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` compiles because `body` comes from an untyped `response.json()` (effectively `any`), subsequent usages such as `backupCodes.map((code) => ...)` and `formatBackupCode(code)` lose type checking on `code`, which should be `string`. This removes compile-time protection against passing the wrong shape and can mask bugs if the API response shape changes.

findings.title: Backup codes Blob URL is never revoked when the modal is closed/unmounted
findings.body: `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is only revoked the next time `handleSetup` succeeds (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl);`, line 98). If the user never re-runs setup (e.g., completes 2FA setup once and later reopens/cancels the modal, or navigates away), the created object URL is never revoked, causing a memory leak that persists until the page is reloaded.
